nodes.title: ProjectBundle
nodes.description: The canonical, schema-versioned interchange document defined in @arkaik/schema: one project plus its nodes, edges, and an optional embedded journal, parsed and validated on every import and write.

nodes.title: Two axes: status is delivery, stage is exposure
nodes.description: Node status stays a pure delivery lifecycle; exposure concerns live on the separate stage axis instead of being folded into status.

metadata.context: Early proposals for the status overhaul considered adding `limited` and `deprecated` as statuses in their own right, but that would have conflated exposure — how visible or available a node is — with delivery lifecycle, where a node sits in the build pipeline.
metadata.consequences: The stage axis keeps expressing exposure on its own terms; the status list stays a clean seven-value delivery lifecycle with no exposure concepts mixed in; `limited` and `deprecated` were rejected as statuses and never entered the vocabulary.

nodes.title: Blocked is a flag, not a status
nodes.description: A blocked node keeps its lifecycle status; blockage is recorded as a metadata flag instead of a status value.

metadata.context: A blocked node parked in a dedicated `blocked` status lost its lifecycle position the moment it got blocked — there was no way to tell whether it had been in backlog or in development.
metadata.consequences: `metadata.blocked_by` now carries the dependency reference directly; a blocked node keeps its underlying status untouched; the node library filters on the flag rather than on a separate status value.

nodes.title: Status migrations: hard cutover + permanent aliases
nodes.description: The v2-to-v3 status vocabulary remap runs once, at import, with the retired ids accepted forever afterward as parse-time aliases.

metadata.context: Soft-deprecating the old ids (`prioritized`, `blocked`, and the pre-v3 meaning of `backlog`) would have left every consumer — the app, the CLI, the MCP server — carrying dual-vocabulary branches forever.
metadata.consequences: A one-time, version-gated remap runs on any bundle below schema_version 3 and stamps the new version; the retired ids `prioritized` and `blocked` are accepted as permanent parse-time aliases from then on; journal history is never rewritten, so historical events keep their original vocabulary.

nodes.title: Project
nodes.description: The root identity of a bundle: id, title, optional version label, root_node_id, and metadata carrying maps, map display overrides, and product definitions.

nodes.title: Node
nodes.description: The atomic graph unit: one of six species (flow, view, data-model, api-endpoint, acceptance, decision) with a title, lifecycle status, platforms, and species-specific metadata.

nodes.title: Edge
nodes.description: A typed directed relationship between two nodes — composes, calls, displays, queries, covers, supersedes, generates, or impacts — validated against per-type source/target rules.

nodes.title: JournalEvent
nodes.description: A ULID-identified, append-only history event (node.created, node.status_changed, release.tagged, deliverable.shipped, ...) with timestamp and actor; history only ever grows.

nodes.title: MapDefinition
nodes.description: A saved map stored in project.metadata.maps: kind (journey or system), species and edge-type filters, root anchor, product scope, layout hints, and card display options.

nodes.title: Product
nodes.description: A ProductDefinition in project.metadata.products that scopes flows, views, and acceptances into one product; membership for other species is derived by traversal.

nodes.title: Deliverable
nodes.description: A projection computed from deliverable.shipped journal events: one unit of shipped work (typically a merged PR) with a summary, URL, and touched node ids, sitting between events and releases.

nodes.title: projects
nodes.description: IndexedDB (Dexie) store with one row per local project, keyed by project id, holding the journal-less BundleSnapshot so a mutation rewrites only that project's row.

nodes.title: journals
nodes.description: IndexedDB (Dexie) store with one row per project holding its embedded journal events; appends grow this row without ever re-serializing the graph snapshot.

nodes.title: meta
nodes.description: Small IndexedDB key/value store for local-provider bookkeeping — currently just the one-time legacy localStorage migration flag.

nodes.title: publik_snapshots
nodes.description: Postgres table of immutable anonymous shares: the journal-stripped, schema-validated bundle as jsonb plus an owner-key hash, size, and report count; re-publishing creates a new id.

nodes.title: publik_rate_limits
nodes.description: Postgres table of append-only throttle rows keyed by HMAC-hashed IP and action, counted over a sliding 1-hour window and pruned opportunistically — rate limiting with no Redis.

nodes.title: users
nodes.description: Auth.js adapter table of signed-in users, extended by arkaik with a tier column that selects the row in the TIER_LIMITS enforcement table.

nodes.title: accounts
nodes.description: Auth.js adapter table linking OAuth provider identities (GitHub at launch) to users, holding the provider's token response per linked account.

nodes.title: sessions
nodes.description: Auth.js adapter table for database sessions; unused on the request path because the session strategy is JWT, but created for adapter-schema completeness.

nodes.title: verification_token
nodes.description: Auth.js adapter table for email magic-link verification tokens; the email provider is deferred, so the table exists for adapter-contract completeness.

nodes.title: synk_projects
nodes.description: Postgres table with one row per backed-up local project, keyed by the composite (user_id, client project id) so two users can back up projects that share an id.

nodes.title: synk_backups
nodes.description: Postgres table of retained backup versions: the full bundle with journal as jsonb plus a server-computed sha256 for content-hash dedupe, pruned by retention per tier.

nodes.title: owners
nodes.description: Postgres table for the tenancy seam every hosted resource hangs off: today one derived personal owner per user (own-u<id>), forward-compatible with org owners.

nodes.title: owner_members
nodes.description: Postgres membership table joining users to owners with a role; getCaller resolves a caller's owner ids through it on every authenticated request.

nodes.title: api_tokens
nodes.description: Postgres table of machine credentials (ark_<prefix>_<secret>): a clear unique prefix for one-read lookup, a sha256 hash of the secret, scoped permissions, and revocation/expiry timestamps.

nodes.title: graph_projects
nodes.description: Postgres table of hosted product graphs: an owner-scoped jsonb snapshot (project + nodes + edges, no journal) with an optimistic-concurrency version bumped on every accepted mutation.

nodes.title: graph_events
nodes.description: Postgres append-only journal for hosted projects, keyed (project_id, event ULID) with a bigserial seq as the authoritative ordering — the server twin of the IndexedDB journals store.

nodes.title: project_repos
nodes.description: Postgres table linking hosted projects to the GitHub repositories that implement them, with an optional platform and a path_prefix so one monorepo can scope different subtrees to different platforms.

nodes.title: github_deliveries
nodes.description: Postgres webhook-delivery ledger: claiming a delivery id before applying it makes GitHub retries and manual redelivers idempotent, and rows older than a day are pruned on write.

nodes.title: GET/POST /api/auth/*
nodes.description: Auth.js catch-all route handling sign-in, the GitHub OAuth callback, and session reads; its adapter writes users and linked accounts on sign-in.

nodes.title: GET /api/auth/status
nodes.description: Client-facing auth status: returns whether auth is configured plus the signed-in user's public profile from the JWT session, never touching the database.

nodes.title: POST /api/github/webhook
nodes.description: The one endpoint accepting signed third-party requests: verifies the GitHub App HMAC over raw bytes, claims the delivery id for replay protection, then applies pull-request transitions to linked hosted projects.

nodes.title: GitHub API
nodes.description: Third-party surface arkaik calls back into: the OAuth token exchange during sign-in, and the App-authenticated pulls/{number}/files read that path-scoped monorepo links need.

nodes.title: GET/POST /api/graph/projects
nodes.description: Lists the caller's hosted graph projects and creates new ones from a validated bundle, enforcing the tier's project cap and seeding the event log.

nodes.title: GET/PATCH/DELETE /api/graph/projects/{id}
nodes.description: Reads one hosted project's snapshot, updates its project-level fields (journaling the change), or archives it — always scoped to the caller's owners.

nodes.title: GET /api/graph/projects/{id}/nodes
nodes.description: Read-only listing of a hosted project's nodes out of the stored snapshot, behind the shared graph:read guard chain.

nodes.title: GET /api/graph/projects/{id}/edges
nodes.description: Read-only listing of a hosted project's edges out of the stored snapshot, behind the shared graph:read guard chain.

nodes.title: GET /api/graph/projects/{id}/journal
nodes.description: Returns a hosted project's append-only journal in server seq order from the graph_events table.

nodes.title: GET /api/graph/projects/{id}/export
nodes.description: Assembles and returns the full ProjectBundle — snapshot plus journal — for download or migration back to local-first storage.

nodes.title: POST /api/graph/projects/{id}/mutations
nodes.description: The single write path for hosted graphs: applies validated mutation ops to the snapshot, bumps the concurrency version, and appends the emitted journal events atomically.

nodes.title: GET/POST/DELETE /api/graph/projects/{id}/repos
nodes.description: Manages a hosted project's repository links — repo, optional platform, optional monorepo path prefix — after checking the project belongs to the caller.

nodes.title: POST /api/publik
nodes.description: Publishes an anonymous, immutable snapshot: strips the journal, validates the bundle, stores it under a fresh id, and returns a one-time owner key — rate-limited per hashed IP.

nodes.title: GET/DELETE /api/publik/{id}
nodes.description: Serves a shared snapshot's bundle to anyone with the link, and deletes it for a caller presenting the matching owner key (verified against its stored hash).

nodes.title: POST /api/publik/{id}/report
nodes.description: Flags a shared snapshot by incrementing its report count, rate-limited per hashed IP like snapshot creation.

nodes.title: GET /api/synk/projects
nodes.description: Lists the signed-in user's backed-up projects with their latest backup info, read from the user-scoped Synk tables.

nodes.title: PUT/DELETE /api/synk/projects/{id}
nodes.description: Uploads a backup version of a local project — validated, sha256-deduped, journal included, tier limits enforced — or deletes the project and cascades away all its backups.

nodes.title: GET /api/synk/projects/{id}/backups
nodes.description: Lists the retained backup versions of one of the user's projects, newest first, without re-parsing the stored bundles.

nodes.title: GET /api/synk/backups/{id}
nodes.description: Downloads one backup's full bundle (journal intact) for restore, scoped to the session user's own rows.

nodes.title: GET /api/synk/ping
nodes.description: Minimal session-guarded probe — 401 without a session, otherwise ok plus the user — the template every authenticated service handler copies.

nodes.title: GET/POST /api/tokens
nodes.description: Session-only token management: lists an owner's API tokens and mints new scoped ones, returning the plaintext secret exactly once — a bearer token can never mint another token.

nodes.title: DELETE /api/tokens/{id}
nodes.description: Revokes an API token by stamping revoked_at, after verifying the session user belongs to the token's owner.

nodes.title: Create Project Dialog
nodes.description: Modal form capturing a title and optional description for a new empty project, destined for whichever section opened it.

nodes.title: Maps Index

nodes.title: System Map Canvas
nodes.description: The model-centered canvas joining views, API endpoints, and data models by cross-layer edges, with an organic/tiered layout switch, a hover-and-pin neighborhood spotlight that dims everything outside one node's relations, and the same minimap.

nodes.title: Map Editor Dialog
nodes.description: Dialog for authoring a custom map definition — id, title, kind, species and edge filters, root anchor picked from the project's nodes, product scope, depth, and layout hints.

nodes.title: Map Display Popover

nodes.title: Command Palette

nodes.title: Keyboard Shortcuts Dialog

nodes.title: Adjust Map Display

nodes.title: Edit Node Details

nodes.title: Browse Library

nodes.title: Changelog

nodes.title: History

nodes.title: Decision Log

nodes.title: Delivery Board

nodes.description: Trace exactly what happened and when by browsing the full journal event feed and narrowing it to one event family.

nodes.description: Record a product decision from the Decision Log — name the What, then fill in context, consequences, status, and decided date in its editor.

nodes.title: Track Delivery Status
nodes.description: Follow work across the lifecycle on the delivery board, filtering by platform, species, or search to find and update the items that matter.

nodes.title: Public Snapshot Page

nodes.title: Publish Dialog

nodes.title: Publish to Publik
nodes.description: Share a project anonymously: confirm what becomes public, publish the bundle (journal stripped server-side), save the one-time owner key, and open the unlisted snapshot page.

nodes.title: Value coverage at a glance

nodes.title: Bulk selection stays honest

nodes.title: Doc health always visible

nodes.title: History Never Rewritten

nodes.title: Filter History by Family

nodes.title: Design and Delivery Apart

nodes.title: Deliverables Anchor When Shipped

nodes.title: Unreleased Work Stays Visible

nodes.title: Decisions Keep Their Why

Then reopening the decision later shows the same why, how, and date

nodes.title: Decision Edits Save Themselves

nodes.title: Superseded Decisions Stay Traceable

Then A appears nested and dimmed under B rather than removed, and opening A still shows its full record

nodes.title: Publish without an account

nodes.title: Failed backups lose nothing

nodes.title: Restore never overwrites

nodes.title: Moving keeps local copy

nodes.title: Token secret shown once

nodes.title: Sign-in never gates local

nodes.title: The journal is an append-only JSONL sidecar, merged by git union
nodes.description: History lives in a journal.jsonl file next to the snapshot, one self-contained event per line, never inside the bundle. Appending is the only write verb.

metadata.context: Status was a mutable field that forgets, and the product needed timelines, changelogs and release notes without bloating or endangering the snapshot. Agents are the primary writers, and whole-file JSON regeneration invites the corrupt-the-whole-file failure mode. JSONL is the one shape where git's union merge is sound: concurrent appends merge automatically and order is recoverable from the events themselves.
metadata.consequences: `arkaik init` configures `merge=union` for the sidecar, so parallel branches never conflict on history. A malformed line invalidates exactly one event — the validator reports the line number — and can never damage existing history or the snapshot. Embedded `journal[]` exists only as a projection for transport (import, Publik, LLM output), not as a storage recommendation.

nodes.title: Snapshot authoritative for state, journal for history — never event sourcing
nodes.description: The snapshot is the source of truth for current state and the journal for how it got there; v1 makes no replay promises and consumers never re-project one from the other.

metadata.context: With two records of the graph, one had to win. Event sourcing would make the journal primary and force replay guarantees, merge semantics and migration of every historical event shape — machinery the product does not need. Per-node timestamps do not exist and clocks lie, so any reconciliation had to work by value.
metadata.consequences: Every writer dual-writes: patch the snapshot and append the matching event in the same change. The validator cross-checks the two by value — the last status_changed.to must equal the current status — and any mismatch is a named validation error. Divergence is repaired explicitly by appending corrective events (the snapshot wins); silently re-projecting would launder drift instead of surfacing it.

nodes.title: History is never rewritten; legacy ids are accepted forever
nodes.description: Journal events, once written, are never edited or migrated. Historical events may carry retired vocabulary (like the pre-v3 status ids) and every validator must accept them indefinitely.

metadata.context: An append-only log is only trustworthy if it is actually immutable — a history that gets rewritten on every vocabulary change is a cache, not a record. Rewriting archives would also break the union-merge model and invalidate compacted release archives. The alternative, migrating old events on read, quietly forges what actually happened.
metadata.consequences: Vocabulary changes ship as permanent read-side aliases, not history rewrites: validators must accept `prioritized`/`blocked` in old `node.status_changed` events forever. Unknown event types and fields are preserved on rewrite and ignored on read, so the vocabulary grows without version bumps. This is a standing decision of the self-map program: do not re-litigate.

nodes.title: IDs are deterministic and human-readable, derived from titles
nodes.description: Node ids are a species prefix plus the kebab-cased title (F-onboarding, DM-bounce), with deterministic disambiguation on collision — never random UUIDs.

metadata.context: Bundles live in git and are written by agents in separate sessions: random ids make every diff noisy and force a lookup table between the map and any conversation about it. A human or agent should be able to predict the id of "Checkout view" without opening the file. The app originally violated this with UUID suffixes, recorded as a defect until the app adopted the convention.
metadata.consequences: Ids double as stable references in prose, PRs and journal events. Renaming a title does not change the id; changing an id means repointing every edge, playlist reference and root_node_id in the same change. Title collisions disambiguate deterministically with a semantic suffix or a counter, and a duplicate id is an import-rejecting error.

nodes.title: Local-first: the browser owns the data, and sign-in never gates it
nodes.description: Projects live in the browser's IndexedDB store by default. Every editing feature works without an account, a server, or a network connection.

metadata.context: The try-it path had to be zero-friction: a Try Lokal button, no sign-up, full editor. Making the server the system of record would have coupled the core product to accounts and infrastructure before either earned their place, and the vision's design rule is that every layer above the format is opt-in convenience.
metadata.consequences: Lokal is not a tier — it is the default. The store graduated from localStorage to IndexedDB via Dexie (with a one-time legacy import) to hold per-project journals without inflating every write. Services degrade to absent when their env vars are unset: the app must boot and serve every local-first surface regardless. Sign-in adds capabilities; it never rearranges or gates local projects.

nodes.title: Publik publishes journal-stripped by default, enforced server-side
nodes.description: Publishing a snapshot to Publik removes the journal unless the request explicitly opts in — and the strip happens on the server, never trusting the client to do it.

metadata.context: A snapshot is what you chose to share; the journal is how you got there — actors, timestamps, abandoned ideas, internal back-and-forth. A privacy default that depends on client behavior alone fails the moment a CLI flag is forgotten, and history leaking through a forgotten flag is not an acceptable failure mode.
metadata.consequences: POST /api/publik removes `journal[]` server-side unless `?include_journal=true` is passed explicitly. Synk backups are the deliberate opposite — they are the user's private data, so history rides along and restores round-trip intact. Publik snapshots stay immutable: no update endpoint, re-publishing mints a new id.

nodes.title: Synk is one-way-up backup, deduped by content hash — not sync
nodes.description: Synk uploads whole bundles on a debounced interval and never writes server state into the local store unprompted. Identical content, detected by canonical-form SHA-256, stores nothing.

metadata.context: Real two-way sync means conflict resolution and journal-based merge — a hard problem the free tier had no business pretending to solve. The browser stays the source of truth for every tier, so the honest free offering is backup: the server stores what the client sent, verbatim, and is never the system of record. Canonical serialization makes "did anything change?" a byte comparison.
metadata.consequences: The client hashes the canonical bundle and the server skips the write when it matches the latest stored hash. Restore is an explicit user action that imports a version as a new local project through the existing collision handling — it never overwrites. Retention prunes on write (no cron), always keeping the newest backup per project regardless of age.

nodes.title: The agent plane is an MCP server with validator-gated dual-writes
nodes.description: Agents reach the map through arkaik-mcp tools — the same projections humans see as pages — and every mutating tool validates the mutated bundle before writing anything.

metadata.context: An agent asked "what's blocked on iOS?" should not parse a 4,000-line JSON file into context or shell out to a CLI with flags. The audience-symmetry principle demanded every human surface have an agent-consumable twin produced by the same schema functions. Free-form file edits by agents invite snapshot-without-history drift, so the write path had to enforce the dual-write doctrine structurally.
metadata.consequences: Every mutation is applied in memory, its journal events derived by the shared derivation, and `validateBundle` run over the result — any error returns pathed findings and writes nothing. On success the events append to the sidecar (actor arkaik-mcp) and the snapshot rewrites canonically. Repo and hosted backends share one identical tool catalog, so agent behavior cannot drift between modes.

nodes.title: One shared mutation core for every writer
nodes.description: The app, the CLI, the MCP server and the hosted API all apply graph mutations and derive their journal events through the same core in the schema package — with only the actor as a parameter.

metadata.context: By the time hosted projects arrived there were four writers of the same graph, and each private implementation of apply-and-derive was a place for the dual-write doctrine to silently diverge. The event-derivation logic was already pure; keeping copies of it in the app, the MCP server and the server API meant the same edit could produce different histories depending on who made it.
metadata.consequences: Mutation application and event derivation live once in the schema package; the app binds actor arkaik-app, the MCP server arkaik-mcp, the GitHub App github-app. A new writer gets the doctrine by construction rather than by discipline. The hosted mutations endpoint takes ops — intents — and replays them through this same core under a row lock.

nodes.title: Hosted projects: the server is the system of record — boundary crossed on purpose
nodes.description: For a project moved into an account, the server owns the graph and mutates it directly, deliberately breaking the "browser is the source of truth" rule that still holds everywhere else.

metadata.context: The browser cannot be the system of record for a graph that a coding agent in any repository and a GitHub webhook both write to. Keeping it there would have required two-way sync, conflict resolution and merge — exactly the problem the services boundaries deferred — to deliver a feature whose whole point is that there is one copy. The crossing was recorded in the spec rather than quietly edited, because the boundary is load-bearing everywhere else.
metadata.consequences: Every server mutation passes the same validateBundle in the same transaction and is refused whole on any error; every change lands as a journal event with a real actor, so history says what acted. Synk and Publik are unchanged. The cost, stated plainly: hosted projects do not work offline — local-first projects still do, and remain the default, with export always available.

nodes.title: Move to account is a copy, never a move
nodes.description: Promoting a local project to a hosted one copies it: the hosted copy gets a new server-owned prj_ id and the local original stays exactly where it is.

metadata.context: Promotion crosses a trust boundary — from data the browser owns to data a server owns — and a destructive move would make trying the hosted feature a one-way door. Hosted projects also do not work offline, so destroying the local original would trade capability for capability. Nothing should be lost if the user changes their mind.
metadata.consequences: The local project keeps working untouched after promotion; the hosted copy lives under a fresh prj_ id with an In your account badge. The same posture repeats across the product — Synk restore imports as a new project, Publik recipients import copies — so no arkaik surface ever destructively relocates a user's graph.

nodes.title: Products are an axis on one graph, not separate projects
nodes.description: A family of apps sharing one substrate is modeled as product definitions in project metadata, with membership stored on flows and views — never as one project per app.

metadata.context: A project was implicitly one product on three hardcoded platforms, so a web-only admin app showed phantom iOS tabs and dragged down Android delivery numbers it was never part of. Splitting into one project per app was rejected: the shared substrate — data models and endpoints — is the norm, and the cross-product traversal is exactly what the graph exists to answer.
metadata.consequences: Products live at project.metadata.products; flows, views and acceptances store membership while data models and endpoints derive it by reachability. node.platforms stays authoritative, every surface picks its shape from the scope's platform arity, and a bundle with no products key behaves exactly as before — no migration, no new concepts. All product validation findings are warnings, so a product decision can never fail CI.

nodes.title: Anchorless acceptances are intake, not floating NFRs
nodes.description: An acceptance with no covers edges is an idea filed before its flows and views exist — a triage state waiting to be attached or decomposed, not a cross-cutting requirement that applies everywhere.

metadata.context: A PM filing "therapist can export session notes" knows which app it is for before knowing which screens it needs, so the model had to admit acceptances before anchors. Reading absent anchors as applies-everywhere would duplicate noise across every product scope; reading stored membership as out-voting the graph would let an acceptance claim a product none of its anchors belong to.
metadata.consequences: Anchors win: a covered acceptance derives its products from what it covers, and stored membership is read only when it covers nothing. Unanchored acceptances surface under All products as an inbox, with a validator warning rather than an error. The workflow shipped as attach, detach, create and split operations, with context carried through each split.

nodes.title: Idea stays a status
nodes.description: An idea is the first stage of the delivery lifecycle, not a separate species or a journal-only artifact. Revisited during the decisions-species work and deliberately re-parked.

metadata.context: When the decision species arrived, ideas were the obvious next candidate for extraction — the journal already has idea.proposed events. But a node at status idea is a real node with a place in the graph: it renders as a ghost, participates in maps, and commits into discovery and backlog. Extracting it would split "things we might build" across two mechanisms with no reader benefit.
metadata.consequences: The 7-status lifecycle keeps idea as its entry point, and the changelog's Design panel reads commitments as idea to discovery to backlog transitions. journal idea.proposed events remain the pre-node intake channel and can link to a node once one exists. The question stays answerable later — this was a re-park, not a never.

nodes.title: The self-map ships as an in-memory sandbox seed, reset on refresh
nodes.description: Arkaik's own map is a default public project served by an in-memory seed provider behind the provider seam: every mutation succeeds in per-tab memory, and refresh restores the pristine seed.

metadata.context: The public self-map had to feel like the real product — read-only or display-tweaks-only were rejected because a graph browser you cannot edit demonstrates nothing. But persisting visitor edits to a shared public project is nonsense, and a shadow IndexedDB copy or a server-hosted project would each drag in machinery the page does not need.
metadata.consequences: A seed DataProvider deep-clones the build-time-imported seed bundle through the normal migrate path, serves reads from memory, and lets every mutator succeed in memory — so all existing hooks, editors and journal appends behave identically, and the History page demonstrates itself. Two tabs are two sandboxes; a banner states the rules and offers Reset and Import a copy; the reserved id can never be squatted by an import.

journal.title: arkaik-mcp installs cleanly from npm
journal.summary: The agent server is now truly one command away: the 0.1.2 release fixes the earlier broken publishes, so `npx -y arkaik-mcp` downloads a working, dependency-free server every time.

journal.notes: Curated maps and a system view join the canvas, an overview dashboard lands, and arkaik-mcp gives agents a first-class way in.

journal.title: Build a flow and its playlist in one go
journal.summary: Agents can now create or update a flow with a full playlist in a single step — the connecting edges are synthesized automatically, so a flow never gets stuck half-made behind a validation deadlock.

journal.title: Map endpoints that call other endpoints
journal.summary: An API endpoint can now call other endpoints on your map — just right for a backend route that fans out to several internal or external APIs, drawn on the System map.

journal.title: Icons wobble like they're hand-drawn
journal.summary: Every icon in Arkaik now carries a subtle hand-drawn distortion, and gently boils to life while you hover or focus its row, card, or menu item. Calm at rest, and it stays still if you prefer reduced motion.

journal.title: Acceptances arrive: promises you can test
journal.summary: Arkaik gains a fifth species — the acceptance, a small testable promise with a Given/When/Then for the how, value tags for the why, and a status per platform. Views, flows, and the product become honest aggregates of what's actually promised.

journal.title: See which platform is late on which promise
journal.summary: The new Acceptances page lays every promise out in a parity matrix — one status column per platform, an amber marker wherever one platform lags. Filter by platform, status, value, or gaps (the URL is shareable), and edit an acceptance right in its panel.

journal.title: Arkaik gets a proper app icon
journal.summary: A fresh favicon plus Apple touch and app icons, so Arkaik looks the part in your tabs, bookmarks, and on your home screen.

journal.title: The Value Pyramid — and gauges that tell the truth
journal.summary: A new Pyramid page shows how well each of the 30 value elements is delivered, per platform and grouped by tier — click one to see the acceptances behind it. And every view, flow, and product gauge now reflects its covering acceptances, with new Parity and Pyramid cards on the Overview.

journal.title: The Arkaik logo comes alive
journal.summary: On the home page, the wordmark now shimmers with a gentle hand-drawn boil — its edges quiver like wet ink. It freezes politely if you prefer reduced motion.

journal.title: Faster paths to help, sign-in, and the details
journal.summary: Jump to the docs straight from the sidebar or the home page, sign in from the project switcher without leaving your work, and the library now opens as a tidy list by default. Long node details finally scroll instead of getting clipped.

journal.title: A living backdrop on the home page
journal.summary: Drifting ASCII mountains now animate quietly behind the hero — adapting to light and dark mode, and holding perfectly still if you prefer reduced motion.

journal.title: Know what each value actually means
journal.summary: All 30 value elements now come with a short plain-language definition — visible right on the Pyramid page, and as a tooltip wherever you pick or read a value on an acceptance.

journal.title: Delivery board icons show their true colors
journal.summary: The status icon on each Delivery column heading now wears its status color instead of rendering plain black.

journal.title: Filters you can scan at a glance
journal.summary: The status, value, and platform filters on the Acceptances page now show each option's icon — and the status's color — so you can spot the right one without reading every label.

journal.notes: Acceptances become first-class: Given/When/Then promises anchored to surfaces and wired to the value they serve, crowned by the Pyramid.

journal.title: One shared mutation core for every writer
Hosted projects: the server is the system of record — boundary crossed on purpose
Move to account is a copy, never a move
Create tokens for your terminal and your agents
journal.summary: A new settings page lets you mint access tokens — the key your coding agent or CI uses to reach your projects. Copy it once, revoke it whenever you like.

journal.title: Your projects can now live in your account
journal.summary: Create a project that lives with your account instead of only in this browser — the same map is there on another machine, and your coding agent can reach it too.

journal.title: Edit your account's projects right in the app
journal.summary: Projects that live in your account open and edit just like local ones, side by side in your list. And when you're ready, you can move a browser project into your account — the local original stays put.

journal.title: Point your coding agent at your Arkaik project
journal.summary: Run one command in any repo and your coding agent can read and update that project's map while it works — no copying files around, no export/import dance.

journal.title: Your acceptances tick themselves off as you ship
journal.summary: Mention an acceptance in a pull request and it moves to in-progress on its own — then to shipped when the PR merges, on the platform that repository builds for.

journal.title: Tell a pull request which platform it shipped
journal.summary: Write AC-guest-checkout@ios in a pull request and only iOS moves — handy when one repository builds several apps. When arkaik can't tell which platform you meant, it says so instead of guessing and marking everything shipped.

journal.title: One repository, several apps, no extra typing
journal.summary: Link a monorepo once per app folder and arkaik works out which app a pull request touched from the files it changed. Your acceptances move on the right platform without anyone remembering to say so.

journal.title: The arkaik CLI is installable now
journal.summary: The command-line tool could not be installed at all, and the published MCP server was an old build that quietly ignored account projects. Both are fixed, so linking a repository to arkaik works the way the docs say it does.

journal.title: The tools now tell you their real version
journal.summary: The MCP server was announcing an old version number — exactly the wrong clue when checking whether your install can reach account projects. It now reports its true version, and the CLI answers --version too.

journal.notes: Hosted graph projects with agent tokens, the app and MCP speaking to the same store, and PRs that move acceptances on their own.

journal.title: All your projects, right where you left them
journal.summary: The projects list now waits a beat for your account before it draws, so the projects you moved there show up alongside the ones on this device — no more wondering where half of them went.

journal.title: Your projects, sorted by where they live
journal.summary: The projects page now groups everything into Hosted, Synked and Lokal, each with its own way to add a project — so what you create lands exactly where you meant it to. The backup nudge only appears when there is actually something local to back up.

journal.title: Your agent tokens now have a front door
journal.summary: Agent tokens live with your account, and you can finally reach them straight from the account menu — no more hunting for the URL.

journal.title: A settings page for every project
journal.summary: Repository links and project deletion moved off the projects list into a dedicated Settings page inside each project. The project card is now simply the way in — no delete button lurking next to it.

journal.title: Jump anywhere in your project with ⌘K
journal.summary: Hit ⌘K from any page and type where you want to go — a map, a library, the delivery board, your settings. Tab completes what you started, Enter takes you there.

journal.title: Your value pyramid, readable at a glance
journal.summary: Each value element now shows four progress rings — one overall, one per platform — instead of a stack of status bars. Hover a ring for the full breakdown, switch between cards and a compact list, and filter down to what's covered or what's still missing.

journal.title: Open a node without losing your map
journal.summary: Node details now open in a column beside your map instead of covering it. Follow a reference to go deeper, press Esc to step back one level, and share the link — it remembers where you were.

journal.title: Project navigation now comes first in the sidebar
journal.summary: Overview, Pyramid, Delivery and Changelog are now the first things you see when you open a project, so the main views are always one glance away.

journal.title: Skip the pitch when you're already building
journal.summary: Signed-in visitors now land straight on their projects instead of seeing the landing page again.

journal.title: Every map can look the way it needs to
journal.summary: Maps now open on the ring charts you know from the Pyramid, and each map remembers its own look — screenshots on or off, platforms as rings or bars, chips or rows. Your walkthrough map and your delivery map are finally allowed to disagree.

journal.title: Products are an axis on one graph, not separate projects
Anchorless acceptances are intake, not floating NFRs
Search the docs with ⌘K
journal.summary: The documentation now has the same command palette as the project view. Type to find any page by its title or filename, press Enter to jump there.

journal.title: A steadier place to work
journal.summary: Opening a panel no longer nudges the page around, every screen names where you are instead of repeating the project name, and everything you can do to a project now sits in one menu. The raw bundle opens as a side panel from any page, too.

journal.title: One project, several apps — each with its own platforms
journal.summary: Your admin dashboard stops pretending it's missing on iOS. Tell Arkaik which apps live in your project and which platforms each one ships on, and every ring, board and tab reports on the app you're actually looking at.

journal.title: Screens can now show what the server pushes them
journal.summary: A screen that receives live updates — a webhook, a stream, a push — can finally be drawn that way and still import cleanly. And when you link two things on a map, Arkaik only offers the relationships that actually make sense between them.

journal.title: Your project can hold several apps — and now you can say so
journal.summary: Name the apps your project covers — the main app, an admin dashboard, a public API — right from settings. Assign screens and flows as you create them, or move a whole shelf at once from the Library.

journal.title: Scrolling stays put
journal.summary: Swiping across breadcrumbs, tables and boards no longer bounces the page or sends you back a screen, and scrolling past the end of a panel stops there instead of dragging the whole page along. Buttons also stopped highlighting themselves like text when you click them.

journal.title: The page header always says which app you're looking at
journal.summary: When you switch products, every page header updates to name the one you're viewing — 'All products' or a specific app — so you stay oriented as you move around.

journal.title: A keyboard shortcuts cheat sheet, one keystroke away
journal.summary: Press ⌘? (or Ctrl+? on Windows and Linux) anywhere to see every shortcut the app responds to, grouped by where it works — and the sheet stays in sync with what the app actually does.

journal.title: The minimap works — and now it steers
journal.summary: The little map in the corner was showing nothing at all. It now draws your whole product, dims everything outside your current view, and lets you drag it to fly across the map — with node colours by status or by kind, saved per map.

journal.title: Zoom in on one app, one page at a time
journal.summary: Delivery, Pyramid, Acceptances and Library each get their own product picker. Narrow one page to a single app without changing what you see everywhere else — and the link you share carries the setting with it.

journal.notes: Products get declared, filtered, and shown everywhere; the studio gets its polish — command palette, column panels, a minimap you can steer.

journal.title: File ideas before you build them
journal.summary: Acceptances can now start life as intake ideas — write them down first, then attach them to views and flows as those get built, or split one idea into several. The product stays with the idea through every step.

journal.title: Statuses that tell the real story
journal.summary: The lifecycle gets clearer: a new Discovery stage for things being shaped, Backlog now means genuinely ready to start, and blocked items keep their place — marked with a small red flag instead of losing their spot in the journey.

journal.title: Your product's decisions, on the map
journal.summary: Arkaik now records decisions — the why, the what, and the consequences — right next to the screens and flows they shaped. Browse them in the new Decision Log, and see at a glance when one decision replaced another.

journal.title: Milestones between deliverables and releases
journal.description: A middle grouping — named milestones that collect deliverables before a release tags them. Parked during the decisions-species cycle; the changelog's era grouping may already cover most of it.

journal.title: Your changelog now tells two stories: what you decided, and what you shipped
journal.summary: The changelog splits into a Design side (open ideas, commitments, decisions) and a Delivery side (releases with the actual deliverables inside them). The play-by-play event feed gets its own History page, and anything blocked now wears a little amber dot.

journal.title: Take Arkaik's own map for a spin — no account needed
journal.summary: A new Explore section on the projects page opens the live map we use to build Arkaik. Poke around, move things, edit freely — it's a sandbox, and a refresh puts everything back. Like what you made? Import a copy and keep it.

journal.notes: The self-map program: a modern status lifecycle, decision records, a changelog split into Design and Delivery, and Arkaik's own map as a public sandbox.

journal.title: Give Pebbles its own real history
journal.description: Retro-populate the Pebbles example bundle with deliverables, releases, and decisions the way the self-map now has them, so both examples demonstrate the full changelog.

journal.title: A platform id for non-web surfaces
journal.description: Toolchain surfaces (CLI, MCP, skill) currently claim web because the platform enum has no terminal or agent value; a dedicated platform id would let the map say what they really are.

journal.title: The self-map ships as an in-memory sandbox seed, reset on refresh
